uncited: This family encompasses methods that offload the computationally intensive sampling and compositing stages of direct volume ray casting to the GPU, utilizing programmable shaders and texture hardware to achieve interactive frame rates [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].

It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based ray casting by exploiting the intrinsic parallelism of fragment processors and efficient inter-pass communication via texture render targets [7443-volume-ray-casting-on-graphics-hardware.md].

It differs from [Shear-Warp](shear-warp.md) by avoiding the final warp step and performing classification after resampling, and from [Custom Hardware Units](8284-custom-hardware-units.md) by relying on general-purpose programmable GPUs rather than dedicated ASICs [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].
All methods in this family implement the emission-absorption optical model defined in [Direct volume ray casting](19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md).
The core pipeline for each pixel consists of ray generation, hardware-accelerated sampling, classification, and compositing [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].

**Ray Generation**: Rays are generated per-pixel, typically by computing ray parameters from camera matrices in vertex/fragment shaders or by rendering the volume's bounding box geometry to determine entry/exit points [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].
**Hardware-Accelerated Sampling**: Scalar volume values are sampled using the GPU's texture hardware.

The volume data is stored in 3D texture memory, and the texture engine performs trilinear interpolation of the eight surrounding voxels in parallel, avoiding manual shader interpolation [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].
**Fragment Shader Compositing**: The ray marching loop, including classification and front-to-back compositing, is executed within the fragment shader [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].
**Early Ray Termination (ERT)**: Rays are terminated when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold (typically 0.95 or 1.0) to optimize performance [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].
This is overcome by using incremental pre-integration tables as presented by Weiler et al. [WKME03].
Rendering and training avoid blending by ensuring sample intervals do not extend beyond tile boundaries.
The shift from CPU-based to GPU-based volume rendering began in the early 2000s with the advent of programmable graphics pipelines (e.g., DirectX 9, OpenGL 2.0).

Early implementations utilized multi-pass rendering techniques to overcome hardware limitations on dependent texture fetches and floating-point precision [7443-volume-ray-casting-on-graphics-hardware.md].

The introduction of 3D texture hardware and fragment shaders allowed for single-pass ray marching, significantly improving performance and enabling interactive visualization [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].

Recent developments focus on scaling these techniques to large datasets using multi-GPU architectures and handling complex data structures like AMR and unstructured meshes [10503-hardware-accelerated-amr-volume-rendering-via-homogenization.md][9631-gpu-based-tiled-ray-casting-with-depth-peeling.md].
